subject: history_social
passage: At Deir el-Medina, the village that housed the workmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs of ancient Egypt, scribes kept records, written on flakes of limestone and broken pottery, of which men were absent from work and why. Many absences are recorded as illness. Historian Yasmin Haddad argues that these entries can largely be taken at face value: in her view, most absences recorded as illness reflected genuine sickness rather than workers taking unofficial days off under a convenient excuse.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Haddad's argument?

choices.A: Absences recorded as illness rose sharply during a period when other records describe an outbreak of eye disease.
choices.B: Absences recorded as illness clustered heavily on the days just before and after religious festivals.
choices.C: The absence records also list other reasons, such as brewing beer or attending to family matters.
choices.D: The village had a physician who was assigned to treat the workmen whenever they fell ill.

explanation.why: Haddad says illness entries mostly reflect real sickness. Real illness strikes at random times, but excuses tend to cluster around days people want off. If illness absences pile up next to festivals, many of them look like extended holidays, which undercuts taking the entries at face value.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Illness absences rising during a documented outbreak is what genuine sickness would produce, so this supports Haddad.
explanation.B: Correct. Illness that clusters around festival days suggests workers were using illness as an excuse to lengthen their time off.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Other recorded reasons show what the records contain but do not reveal whether the illness entries were honest.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Having a physician in the village does not show whether the recorded illnesses were real.
